newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: No absolute right to promotion for women under EU law.
newsitem.headline: No absolute right to promotion for women under EU law.

text.p: A German rule giving women the right to promotion on the grounds that there are fewer women than men in a given grade is not legal under European Union law, a senior European Court adviser said on Thursday.

Advocate General Francis Jacobs gave a non-binding opinion in a case brought by a German teacher against the state of Northrhine-Westphalia for appointing a woman to a post, for which he was equally qualified, on the grounds that there were already more men than women in that grade.

The opinion confirmed the court's ruling in the so-called Kalanke case that any rule which grants women absolute and unconditional priority for appointment or promotion is discriminatory and goes beyond promoting equal opportunities.
The Kalanke case was the first European-wide case dealing with issues of so-called reverse discrimination.

Jacobs told the court that national rules which give women priority for a higher grade position merely because there are fewer women employed in that category, should be struck down as for violating EU rules against employment discrimination.
In a statement issued from the court, he said reverse discrimination was not the issue and it would be inappropriate if it were raised, as that was a policy matter to be determined by legislation.
The court was not being asked to judge the merits of positive discrimination, only whether German national rules promoting the hiring of women conflicted with EU law, he added.
Under the rules of the European Court, Advocates General submit reasoned impartial opinions to the judges to assist them in decision-making.
The opinion is not binding and is not a preliminary ruling. But in a large majority of cases, the reasoning of the opinion is adopted.
